coding_context.description: Giving people an 'accuracy nudge' before showing them headlines make them more discerning about their accuracy and less likely to share false articles on social media
coding_context.reported_success_quote: The first stage of the replication test ( n = 701) was unsuccessful ( p = .67). After collecting a second round of data (additional n = 882, pooled N = 1,583), we found a small but significant interaction between treatment condition and truth discernment (uncorrected p = .017; treatment: d = 0.14, control: d = 0.10). As in the target study, perceived headline accuracy correlated with treatment impact, so that treatment-group participants were less willing to share headlines that were perceived as less accurate.

prior_adjudication.reason: The primary source is confirmed as Roozenbeek, Freeman, and van der Linden (2021, Psychological Science, DOI 10.1177/09567976211024535), a single-study direct replication of Pennycook et al. (2020) Study 2 that explicitly designates the two-stage truth-discernment interaction test as its sole focal test for SCORE purposes. For this focal effect, the authors report that Stage 1 was unsuccessful (p = .67) while the pooled Stage 2 sample replicated the treatment effect (p = .017) with about 50% attenuation, concluding that their findings are in partial agreement with the target study ('mixed').
